## When a Straight Boundary Is Too Simple

A linear SVM uses a score of the form $w^\top x+b$. Its boundary is a straight line in two dimensions. Some class patterns cannot be separated that way.

We can change the features instead. A **feature map** $\phi$ replaces each input $x$ with a new vector $\phi(x)$. We then fit a linear rule in the new coordinates:

$$
f(x)=w^\top\phi(x)+b.
$$

The score is linear in the new features. It may be nonlinear in the original inputs. This distinction is the main idea behind kernel methods.

These notes build on Ying's SVM seminar slides (n.d.). The extra examples make the feature map and its inner product explicit.

## A Small Example Before the Kernel Trick

Suppose $x$ is a real number. The outer points $-2$ and $2$ have label $+1$. The middle points $-1/2$ and $1/2$ have label $-1$.

No threshold on the number line separates both outer points from both inner points. A score $wx+b$ can change sign at most once.

Now use $\phi(x)=x^2$. The positive examples map to $4$. The negative examples map to $1/4$. A threshold at $1$ separates them:

$$
f(x)=x^2-1.
$$

The new feature measures distance from the origin, rather than left-versus-right position. The nonlinear boundary in the original space is $x=\pm1$.

This is a constructed separator. We have not claimed that these particular coefficients solve an SVM training problem. The example shows what a feature map makes possible.

## Inner Products Are the Only Quantities We Need

The [binary SVM dual](linear-svm.qmd) uses the data through $x_i^\top x_j$. After a feature map, this becomes

$$
\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle.
$$

Define a **kernel** by

$$
K(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle.
$$

If we can evaluate $K$ directly, we do not need to construct every coordinate of $\phi(x)$. This is the kernel trick.

We have changed how an inner product is computed. We have not removed the optimisation problem.

## A Quadratic Feature Map We Can Check

For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, consider

$$
\phi(x)=\left(x_1^2,\sqrt2\,x_1x_2,x_2^2\right).
$$

For another point $z=(z_1,z_2)$, its feature-space inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle
&=x_1^2z_1^2+2x_1x_2z_1z_2+x_2^2z_2^2\\
&=(x_1z_1+x_2z_2)^2\\
&=(x^\top z)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $\sqrt2$ is needed. Without it, the middle term would have coefficient one instead of two.

For example, take $x=(1,2)$ and $z=(3,1)$. Directly,

$$
K(x,z)=(3+2)^2=25.
$$

The feature vectors give the same answer:

$$
(1,2\sqrt2,4)\cdot(9,3\sqrt2,1)=9+12+4=25.
$$

This small calculation contains the whole trick. A short formula replaces a longer feature calculation. The benefit can be much larger when the feature vector has many coordinates.

## What Makes a Kernel Valid?

A resemblance score is not automatically a valid inner-product kernel. If $K$ comes from a real feature map, it must be symmetric. For any inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, its **Gram matrix** has entries

$$
G_{ij}=K(x_i,x_j).
$$

It must also be positive semidefinite. This means that, for every real vector $c$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
c^\top Gc
&=\sum_{i,j}c_ic_j\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle\\
&=\left\lVert\sum_i c_i\phi(x_i)\right\rVert^2\ge0.
\end{aligned}
$$

That proof explains the condition without needing a theory of infinite-dimensional spaces. It also links kernels with the positive semidefinite matrices in [convex optimisation](convexity.qmd).

Checking one finite Gram matrix is useful for those points. It does not prove that a proposed formula is a valid kernel for every possible input.

## Common Kernels

### Linear Kernel

$$
K(x,z)=x^\top z.
$$

This uses the original features. A kernel method need not produce a nonlinear boundary.

### Polynomial Kernel

$$
K(x,z)=(\gamma x^\top z+r)^d,
$$

where $d$ is a positive integer, $\gamma>0$, and $r\ge0$. Its expanded features include products of input coordinates. For $r=0$ and $d=2$, the example above shows the map directly when $\gamma=1$.

These coordinate products can express interactions. A linear rule on them can depend on how two original features vary together.

### Gaussian Kernel

$$
K(x,z)=\exp\bigl(-\gamma\lVert x-z\rVert^2\bigr),
\qquad\gamma>0.
$$

Nearby inputs have kernel values close to one. Far-apart inputs have values close to zero. A larger $\gamma$ makes that value fall faster with distance.

This gives a local notion of similarity. The full feature-space construction is beyond these notes. We use the standard Gaussian kernel without proving its validity here.

## The Kernel SVM

For soft-margin classification, replace the inner products in the dual:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_\alpha\quad &\sum_i\alpha_i
-\frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j K(x_i,x_j)\\
\text{subject to}\quad &0\le\alpha_i\le C,
\qquad\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

After training, predict from the sign of

$$
f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i y_iK(x_i,x)+b.
$$

The coefficients can be positive or negative after multiplication by $y_i$. Prediction is therefore not just a vote for the most similar point. It combines weighted contributions from the support vectors.

The Gram matrix is positive semidefinite for a valid kernel. Multiplying its rows and columns by labels $\pm1$ preserves that property. The dual objective remains concave.

## Two Parameters with Different Jobs

For a Gaussian SVM, $C$ and $\gamma$ control different things:

| Parameter | Main Role |
|---|---|
| $C$ | Sets the cost of margin violations relative to the norm penalty. |
| $\gamma$ | Sets how quickly similarity falls with distance. |

A large $\gamma$ permits a boundary that responds to very local patterns. A large $C$ makes fitting the training examples more important. Neither setting guarantees better predictions. Use validation data to choose them together (scikit-learn developers, n.d.).

Feature scaling matters here too. A coordinate measured in large units can dominate $\lVert x-z\rVert^2$. The model then treats that coordinate as more important just because of its scale.

## What the Kernel Trick Does and Does Not Give Us

The trick avoids listing the feature coordinates. Some kernels correspond to an infinite-dimensional feature space. We can still compute each kernel value with a finite formula.

This does not mean that every dataset becomes separable. Identical inputs with opposite labels remain identical under the same feature map. Soft margins still have a role.

It also does not make computation free. A dense Gram matrix has $n^2$ entries. Prediction can require many kernel evaluations when there are many support vectors.

The useful change is in representation. We can choose richer features while keeping the same basic SVM optimisation structure.
